analysis.one_liner: Cuts mercury emissions from power plants, incinerators, cement kilns, and chemical plants by 90–95%.
analysis.headline: The mercury-control bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in December 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required steep cuts in mercury emissions from the country's biggest mercury sources: coal- and oil-burning power plants (at least 90% below 1999 levels), industrial boilers, incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and cement kilns [S2] [S3]. It would also have required labeling of mercury-containing products, their separation from the trash stream, and public reporting of each facility's mercury emissions [S2] [S3]. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond being referred to committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, people who eat fish, pregnant women and their fetuses, young children, and people who rely on self-caught or subsistence fish would benefit most, since mercury exposure happens mainly through contaminated fish [S3]. Communities near the highest mercury deposition areas — the Great Lakes and Ohio River Valley, the Northeast, and parts of the South and Texas — would see fewer emissions from nearby power plants, incinerators, and cement kilns [S3]. The bill would also have required public reporting of facility-by-facility mercury emissions [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families eating fish, pregnant women, children

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least a 90% reduction in mercury emissions from coal- and oil-fired utility and industrial boiler units from 1999 levels
Requires chlor-alkali plants and Portland cement plants to cut their mercury emissions at least 95% below baselines set by the EPA
Requires public, facility-specific reporting of mercury emissions from power plants, boilers, incinerators, and cement plants each year
Requires manufacturers to label mercury-containing products and, three years after enactment, bans their sale without an EPA exemption, with take-back programs for exempted products
Requires plans to separate and remove mercury-containing items such as fluorescent bulbs, batteries, and switches from waste before landfilling or incineration
Bars sale of mercury from the National Defense Stockpile for commercial or industrial use, and funds research on permanently retiring excess mercury

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-burning power plants, industrial boiler operators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, Portland cement plants, solid waste incinerators, and manufacturers of mercury-containing products would bear the cost of installing emission controls, monitoring, labeling, and product take-back programs [S2] [S3]. Some of these costs would likely pass through to electricity and product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning power plants and mercury-using industry

drawbacks.text: The 90–95% cuts across every source category, applied quickly (regulations within 180 days of enactment), would have been costly for utilities and industry, and some of that cost would likely show up in electricity prices and product costs
The bill allowed trading only among units at a single site, not across plants, which raises compliance costs compared with market-wide trading schemes
The three-year product phaseout with EPA exemptions required extensive case-by-case determinations and public hearings for each exempted product
The burden fell on a handful of specific industries while the benefits (less mercury in fish) accrue broadly, which explains why the bill had essentially no industry support

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case was strong: the bill cited the National Academy of Sciences' 2000 finding that mercury exposure harms fetuses and children, and the fact that 41 states had issued fish consumption advisories by 1999, up from 27 in 1993 [S3]. The costs — emission controls, monitoring, and product redesign at power plants, cement kilns, and chemical plants — were real and would have been concentrated on specific industries, with some pass-through to electricity and product prices. The bill was aggressive in its deadlines and its refusal to allow cross-site trading, which an honest supporter would acknowledge made compliance more expensive than necessary. But the core trade was cleaner fish and air for a public that bears the health burden, in exchange for costs borne mainly by the industries that emit the mercury.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing or vote — the quietest way for a bill to die.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 20, 2001, with one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor
Its only action beyond introduction was being read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Power plants, industrial boilers, chlor-alkali plants, cement kilns, and incinerator operators are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided the 90–95% emission cuts, monitoring, and product rules it would have imposed [S3]. Families who eat fish and communities in high-deposition areas did not receive the emission reductions the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and industry avoided compliance costs

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up for consideration after its referral

against.name: Senate majority leadership
against.what_they_did: The bill's only formal action beyond introduction was referral to the committee; no markup, report, or floor scheduling followed

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were on the bill — one Democrat and one Republican — and no votes were ever taken on it.

industries.note: The largest U.S. mercury source would have had to cut emissions at least 90% from 1999 levels, install monitoring, and file enforceable permits [S3]. The industry's interest in avoiding these costs runs against the public's interest in cleaner fish and air.
Mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants would have had to cut emissions at least 95% below baseline and meet enforceable permit requirements [S3].
Cement plants would have had to cut mercury dust emissions at least 95% below baseline and obtain enforceable permits [S3].
The bill would have imposed mercury monitoring, a maximum emission rate, and mandatory controls where rates were exceeded [S3].

industries.industry: Manufacturers and importers of mercury-containing products
industries.note: Three years after enactment, manufacturers could not sell mercury-containing products without an EPA exemption, and would have had to label products and run take-back programs for exempted ones [S3].

industries.industry: Solid waste haulers and facility operators
industries.note: Waste handlers would have had to file and follow plans to separate and remove mercury-containing items like fluorescent bulbs, batteries, thermostats, and switches before disposal [S3].

industries.industry: Defense Department and its mercury stockpile
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited selling National Defense Stockpile mercury for commercial or industrial use, and required a Pentagon report on military mercury use [S3].
